name: Mboum (Ngaoundéré)
autonymMeaning: Ngaoundéré refers to the mountain “with a navel”, which gave the town its name
overview: The Mboum, historical founders of Ngaoundéré, are now a minority there among the Fulani, Gbaya, Hausa, Kanuri and migrants from the South. Strongly Islamised, patrilineal and organised around the chiefdom and the trade guilds, they practise farming, livestock rearing and an ancient craft tradition, to the rhythm of the tam-tam and the balafon.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Minority group in Ngaoundéré, where the Fulani dominate; there it lives alongside the Kaka, Gbaya, Hausa, Kanuri, Nyangeré, Bamiléké and Basaa.
Mboum is also spoken in the Djérem, the Faro-et-Déo, the Vina and the Mayo-Rey.
The group is very mixed: most Mboum marry outside the group.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: The land is ancestral and belongs to the Mboum; Islam consecrates the right of ownership, even if some Mboum now buy their plots.
Tradition has the group coming from Yemen and Arabia, through Egypt and Sudan, as far as Ngaoundéré, which remains the identity reference.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: Patriarchal society organised around a chief and craft guilds: elders are respected, and the large landowner is influential.
Decisions come from the chiefdom and follow Islamic rules.
The former specialised societies have disappeared: anyone can fill all the roles, including funeral rites.
Deference: one does not sit next to the chief. Historical grievances with neighbours remain, but are rarely mentioned.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; it is the wife who joins her husband.
Formerly, parents chose the spouses and polygamy was common; these practices have declined.
One used to become a man through rites, today through circumcision, the complete reading of the Quran and independence.
Steps: request, engagement, then religious bride price (sodok), whose central element is an equivalent in dihad, an old currency that symbolises the union of the two families.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: The old cults have disappeared; religious life is now Islamic.
Birth enriches the family; the dead are accompanied by prayer.
Taboos: eating with the left hand, missing prayer times; for women, disrespect; for children, disobedience and laziness.
Serious offences are severely punished according to religious law; theft, insult and lying call for forgiveness.
Divination: cowries, numerology, geomancy, or consulting the Koran.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Men: crafts, divination, farming and livestock rearing. Women: crafts (embellishing the house), trade, farming and livestock rearing.
The land is passed on by inheritance; the lamido could allocate it. Today it falls under the State.
Ancestral crafts: quivers (karkwa), bows for war, hunting and sport, cotton spinning, weaving.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Men wear boubous and gandouras; women wrappers, boubou and headscarf.
Traditional medicine remains very much alive, considered effective.
Beauty: the robust, powerful man; the full-figured, well-groomed woman, attentive to her husband and a good cook.
Courtship: offering presents and surrounding the family with attention.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Rhythms and dances: mbolo on the tam-tam, ndja on the balafon, mbuyé on the drums (initiation dance); the mbala accompanies all ceremonies.
Old festivals, now abandoned: notably the coming out of the circumcised.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: The Mboum today share a common culture with the Fulani, the Dii and the Hausa.

sections.title: The names
items: Twins (gundaba) receive paired names: Housseina and Housseini, Hassan and Hassana (the -a marks the feminine).
The name is given on the 7th day, at a rite, or according to the circumstances; it does not change, but pseudonyms and titles are customary.
Appellatives: nya for a man, mâ for a woman.

anthroponymes.meaning: <<the one who is born and finds their parent alive>>

lessons.title: Who are the Mboum (Ngaoundéré)? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Mboum (Ngaoundéré) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Mboum (Ngaoundéré) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Mboum (Ngaoundéré) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Mboum (Ngaoundéré) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Mboum (Ngaoundéré) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Mboum (Ngaoundéré) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Minority group at Ngaoundéré, where the Fulani dominate; there it lives alongside Kaka, Gbaya, Haoussa, Kanuri, Nyangeré, Bamiléké and Basaa. • Mboum is also spoken in the Djérem, the Faro-et-Déo, the Vina and the Mayo-Rey. • The group is very mixed: most Mboum marry outside the group. • The land is ancestral and belongs to the Mboum; Islam recognises their right of ownership, even though some Mboum now buy their plots. • Tradition says the group came from Yemen and Arabia, through Egypt and Sudan, to Ngaoundéré, which remains the reference point for identity.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Mboum, historical founders of Ngaoundéré, are now a minority there among the Fulani, Gbaya, Hausa, Kanuri and migrants from the South. Strongly Islamised, patrilineal and organised around the chiefdom and the trade guilds, they practise farming, livestock rearing and an ancient craft tradition, to the rhythm of the tam-tam and the balafon.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Mboum (Ngaoundéré) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-II — Cultural practices: ways of life
lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Mboum (Ngaoundéré)
objectives: Linking food to the living environment

vocabulary.langText: couscous de maïs ou de manioc

lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Mboum (Ngaoundéré), describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Mboum (Ngaoundéré).
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Mboum (Ngaoundéré), describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Mboum (Ngaoundéré).” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: maize or cassava couscous, beef, mutton, fish, sorrel (foléré), baobab leaves. • Drinks: millet beer, porridge, ndzindza (root drink). • Men: crafts, divination, farming and livestock rearing. Women: crafts (embellishing the home), trade, farming and livestock rearing. • Ancestral crafts: quivers (karkwa), bows for war, hunting and sport, cotton spinning, weaving.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Mboum (Ngaoundéré) eat mainly maize or cassava couscous, beef, mutton, fish, foléré, baobab leaves. Traditional drinks: millet beer, porridge, ndzindza. These foods are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Choose a dish of the Mboum (Ngaoundéré): write its sheet (name in the language, ingredients, steps, occasion when it is served).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

steps.instruction: Describe a Mboum (Ngaoundéré) dance (participants, time, instruments, gestures, meaning), then perform it with your group.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Mboum (Ngaoundéré)
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Mboum (Ngaoundéré), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Mboum (Ngaoundéré). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Mboum (Ngaoundéré), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Mboum (Ngaoundéré). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • Men: crafts, divination, farming and livestock. Women: crafts (decorating the house), trade, farming and livestock. • Land is passed on by inheritance; the lamido could allocate some. Today it falls under the State. • Ancestral crafts: quivers (karkwa), bows for war, hunting and sport, cotton spinning, weaving.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Men: crafts, divination, farming and livestock rearing. Women: crafts (embellishing the house), trade, farming and livestock rearing. Land is passed on by inheritance; the lamido could allocate it. It now falls under the State.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a two-column table (men / women) of the Mboum (Ngaoundéré)'s activities, then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Mboum (Ngaoundéré)
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death
lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Mboum (Ngaoundéré), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Mboum (Ngaoundéré). Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Mboum (Ngaoundéré), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Mboum (Ngaoundéré). Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The old cults have disappeared; religious life is now Islamic. • Birth enriches the family; the dead are accompanied by prayer. • Prohibitions: eating with the left hand, missing prayer times; for women, disrespect; for children, disobedience and laziness. • Serious offences are severely punished according to religious law; theft, insult and lying call for forgiveness. • Divination: cowries, numerology, geomancy, or consulting the Koran.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The old cults have disappeared; religious life is now Islamic. Birth enriches the family; the dead are accompanied by prayer.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Mboum (Ngaoundéré) (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Discover what the Mboum (Ngaoundéré) believe, the places they respect and the taboos they observe.

student.memo: The old cults have disappeared; religious life is now Islamic. Birth enriches the family; the dead are accompanied by prayer.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Mboum
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day

vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Mboum (Ngaoundéré) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Mboum (Ngaoundéré) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Mboum (Ngaoundéré) greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Mboum (Ngaoundéré) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • The community's language is Mboum. • Greeting formulae: Mí bâféwá = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); Nà ɓɛ́làke = morning greeting (one person); Àndiɲáɓéláké = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Sóŋ, Dwá, Mə̀kón, ɲə̀m, Ndziɓî. • Terms of address: nya for a man, mâ for a woman. • The Mboum today share a common culture with the Fulani, the Dii and the Hausa.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Mboum are the first steps towards communicating with the Mboum (Ngaoundéré). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Learn to greet, introduce yourself and count in Mboum.

activities.title: I greet
activities.instruction: Learn the greeting formulas for morning, midday and evening.

activities.title: I introduce myself
activities.instruction: Say your name, where you are from and where you live.

activities.title: I count
activities.instruction: Count objects from 1 to 10.

activities.title: I pass on
activities.instruction: Teach a formula to a classmate or a family member.

student.memo: Greeting and counting in Mboum are the first steps towards communicating with the Mboum (Ngaoundéré). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.
